picks.title: The Snickers ice truck is loose in the city
picks.why_trust: To launch the Snickers ice bar in Korea, the brand skipped renting one address and sent a wrapped truck through foot-traffic districts instead, handing out bars with mini games — a curling 'Chill Shot', an ice-freezer photo zone — and merch for anyone who clears a mission. The guerrilla moving-popup format is the trend itself: cooling you down on the spot instead of asking you to queue.
picks.desc: A free ice-bar truck roaming Seoul's busiest districts — the popup comes to you.
picks.desc_kr: 서울 번화가를 돌아다니는 무료 아이스바 트럭 — 팝업이 나를 찾아온다.

picks.title: A creator bakery meets the yogurt empire
picks.why_trust: Parkddugi, a cult creator bakery, joined Yoajung — the yogurt-ice-cream topping franchise Koreans are currently obsessed with — for a limited run: their bestselling churros salt bread turned into an ice-cream cone under honeycomb and choco-shell toppings, sold only at popup counters in Seongsu and department stores. It's the salt-bread-as-canvas trend and the topping economy colliding in one product.
picks.desc: Churros salt bread piled with honeycomb and choco shell — two Korean obsessions in one cone.
picks.desc_kr: 벌집꿀과 초코쉘을 얹은 츄러스 소금빵 — 한국의 두 집착이 콘 하나에.

picks.title: A museum's AI joke became a real gacha toy
picks.title_kr: 박물관의 AI 농담이 진짜 가챠가 됐다
picks.why_trust: The National Agricultural Museum posted AI and 3D renders of tiny fruit-crate 'crop clicker' keyrings as a gag; the comment section demanded them for real, so the museum partnered with NoPlasticSunday — a studio that works in recycled plastic — and released actual gacha keyrings at the museum and online. It's the fansumer pipeline in one clean arc: brand joke, audience demand, real product.
picks.desc: Fake AI-rendered crop-crate keyrings got so many 'make it real' comments the museum actually did.
picks.desc_kr: AI로 만든 가짜 농작물 키링에 '실물로 내달라'는 댓글이 쌓이자 박물관이 진짜로 만들었다.

picks.title: The BAPE monkey wears a barista apron
picks.why_trust: After a first coaster-and-keychain run, Starbucks Korea brought BAPE's Baby Milo back for round two: foldable bags, neck pillows, reusable-cup events, even tumblers you redeem with loyalty stars. The design is the point — a rolling collab engineered for repeat visits over months instead of a one-week frenzy, which is where Korean café collabs are heading.
picks.desc: Baby Milo's second Starbucks Korea run — a collab designed to keep going, not sell out once.
picks.desc_kr: 베이비 마일로의 스타벅스 코리아 2차전 — 한 번 완판이 아니라 계속 이어지게 설계된 콜라보.

picks.title: Han River 5k that doesn't feel like one
picks.why_trust: This is the loop Seoul runners default to — flat, shaded, and it ends at a convenience store for banana milk.

picks.title: Stretching cafés exist here
picks.why_trust: Assisted stretching went mainstream in Seoul before it hit your feed — these studios train staff properly instead of renting out a trend.

picks.title: Namsan stairs before breakfast
picks.why_trust: The sunrise stair crowd is 60-year-old Seoul regulars who've done this daily for decades — you're borrowing their routine, not a tourist trail.

picks.title: Pilates etiquette 101
picks.why_trust: Seoul pilates studios have unspoken rules (grip socks, arrive 10 early, phone away) — these are the ones that welcome first-timers instead of freezing them out.

picks.title: Riverside bike day
picks.why_trust: The public Ttareungi bikes and the river path are genuinely world-class civic infrastructure — no operator is paying anyone to say that.

picks.title: Forest park recovery walk
picks.why_trust: An old rail line turned into a 6km park — it's where the neighborhood actually decompresses, dogs and all. Zero admission, zero catch.

picks.title: Watermelon ice cream, the dessert you make
picks.why_trust: Half a frozen watermelon, milk poured in, scraped with a spoon — the sound went viral before the taste did. Cafés turned it into menus within weeks; that speed is very Seoul.

picks.title: Salt bread will not stop
picks.meta: the dessert canvas of the year
picks.why_trust: Sogeum-ppang started as a plain butter roll; now it is an ice-cream cone, a mango shell, a churros hybrid. Watching one bread mutate monthly is the fastest way to read Korean dessert culture.

picks.title: Mugwort is the next matcha
picks.why_trust: Ssuk (mugwort) is doing what matcha did ten years ago — moving from grandma's rice cake to affogato and tiramisu. It photographs green, tastes earthier, and locals read it as healthy comfort.

picks.title: Sweet potato season is a religion
picks.why_trust: Every October, Korea reorganizes its dessert shelves around goguma — roasted sweet potato brûlée on ice cream, purple-and-yellow palettes, whole café menus. It is Seoul's pumpkin-spice season, and it is better.

picks.title: Ice cream as a luxury accessory
picks.why_trust: Luxury chocolatiers are entering the ice-cream bar market with cosmetics-case packaging — dessert as a visual object you carry, not just eat. Seoul department store basements are where it lands first.

picks.title: The crepe comeback
picks.why_trust: Crepes are back as a visual format — gelato animal heads peeking out of cones, layered fruit walls. It is less about the pancake, more about what the cone lets you build vertically.

picks.title: Autumn means pumpkin injeolmi
picks.why_trust: Korea's autumn pumpkin isn't spice-latte pumpkin — it's danhobak with injeolmi rice cake: chewy, nutty, dusted in bean powder. Whole cakes, bingsu, even sandwich bread carry it now.

picks.title: Hwappu-ball: cosmetics as ASMR
picks.why_trust: Koreans are stacking cosmetics compacts into towers and pressing them for the click — beauty products consumed as tactile ASMR toys. Brands now design packaging for the sound. It explains why K-beauty packaging feels so good in hand.

picks.title: Chocolate-drenched chips broke the convenience store
picks.why_trust: A classic corrugated chip got crushed, thick-coated in chocolate, and promptly sold out nationwide — while a TV clip sent everyone home to pile plain potato chips on tub ice cream. Salty-sweet-crunchy is a competitive sport here, and the convenience store is the arena.

picks.title: The car company's joke ice cream is real
picks.title_kr: 자동차 회사의 만우절 아이스크림이 진짜가 됐다
picks.why_trust: Hyundai posted a fake ice-cream sandwich as a 2022 April Fools gag; the comment section refused to let it die, and four years later it's an actual GS25 product with collectible car stickers inside. Korean brands treat comment sections as R&D — this is the receipt.

picks.title: Hangul Day turns brands into type foundries
picks.title_kr: 한글날, 브랜드들이 서체 회사가 되는 날
picks.why_trust: Every October 9th Korea celebrates its alphabet, and brands answer with typography: burger chains release free Hangul fonts, 15th-century typefaces from museum archives get reprinted on snack boxes, pizza chains swap loanwords for pure-Korean words on the packaging. 2026 is a centennial year for the holiday, so expect it louder than usual.

picks.title: Halloween here is a black cat now
picks.why_trust: Korea's Halloween has gone deliberately soft: black-sesame cakes shaped like cats, ghost-type Pokémon fronting Lotte World's autumn season, black ceramics standing in for fake blood. The register is moody-cute rather than scary — and it photographs better.

picks.title: October is tarte tatin season
picks.why_trust: Seoul patisseries treat autumn apples the French way — slow-cooked, glossy, concentrated. Plated tarte tatin, apple crumble under melting vanilla: comfort-food nostalgia in fine-dining clothes, peaking in October right alongside the apple harvest festivals.

picks.title: A sweet potato is an idol now
picks.why_trust: Kakao spun a literal sweet potato into a character — Chunguma — and within a year it had plushes, emoticons, a tiramisu collab and a skincare line. Watching Korea turn a root vegetable into a celebrity with a merchandise pipeline is the fastest crash course in the character-industrial complex.

picks.title: Cafés keep getting taken over by characters
picks.why_trust: Seoul's café scene runs a rotating cast of character takeovers — a cartoon monkey in a Starbucks barista apron, chain cafés rebuilt into dollhouse dioramas, limited figures drip-released every ten days to engineer revisits. The scarcity choreography is half the show.
